topic.name: Multiplicities of the Roots of Polynomials

question.text: Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x) = 7x^3 + 42x^2$ have multiplicity $2?$
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial.

For this polynomial, we can factor by noting that the greatest common factor of $7x^3$ and $42x^2$ is $7x^2{:}$

\begin{align*} p(x) &=7x^3 + 42x^2\\[3pt] &= 7x^2(x+6) \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

  • The factor $(x+6)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-6$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

question.text: The root of the polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + x^2 - x - 1$ with multiplicity $2$ is $x=$
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:

\begin{align*} p(x) &= x^3 + x^2 - x - 1 \\[5pt] &= x^2(x+1) - (x+1) \\[5pt] &= (x^2-1)(x+1) \\[5pt] &= (x-1)(x+1)(x+1) \\[5pt] &= (x-1)(x+1)^2 \end{align*}

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

  • The factor $(x+1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-1$ has multiplicity $2.$

  • The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-1}$ has multiplicity $2.$

example.title: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Grouping

question.text: The multiplicity of the root $x=3$ in the polynomial $p(x)=x^3 - 6 x^2 + 11 x - 6$ is
question.explanation:
Since $x=3$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-3)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-3)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-3)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division:

$x^3$ $x^2$ $x^1$ $x^0$
$\color{red}3$ $1$ $-6$ $11$ $-6$
$\color{gray}\downarrow$ $3$ $-9$ $6$
$1$ $-3$ $2$ $0$

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{p(x)}{x-3} = x^2 - 3x + 2, \]

which means

\[ p(x) = (x-3) (x^2 - 3x + 2). \]

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

\begin{align*} p(x) &= (x-3)(x-1)(x-2). \end{align*}

The factor $(x-3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=3$ has multiplicity $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1}.$
